source: Chen, Nan et al., "An autonomous single-actuator UAV with omnidirectional field of view, high agility, and collision resistance", Nature Communications, published 21 May 2026, open access, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-73283-x, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-73283-x. First author Nan Chen and corresponding author Fu Zhang, Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Hong Kong; co-authors include Haotian Li, Yunfan Ren, Guozheng Lu, Fangcheng Zhu and Jiarong Lin, also at that department. University announcement: The HKU Lead, 17 Nov 2026, https://lead.hku.hk/en/article/2026/11/hku-engineering-team-develops-omnidirectional-sensing-single-propeller-autonomous-drone/. Invention name PULSAR II, a research prototype with no product, maker or price. Player-facing claims checked against the paper and the HKU announcement: one motor driving two blades through a swashplate-less mechanism; body spin plus a vertically mounted 360° LiDAR yields no unobserved area; before takeoff a partial indoor map, in flight a fuller 3D map and path planning while hovering; autonomous flight over 6 m/s in an underground parking lot (pillars, doorways, overhead pipes) and cluttered woods; all mapping, avoidance and control onboard, with no GPS, motion capture or ground computer; figure-eights and in-air flips with lower tracking error than the conventional controller in the study; carbon-fiber frame and disturbance observer kept flight stable when a ball was dropped on it while hovering and when it flew into and pushed away obstacles; mass 1122.3 g (about 1.12 kg) and measured hover 15 min 50 s (also in the paper, Supplementary Video 10; the HKU announcement quotes the same duration). Limits: LiDAR-inertial odometry may fail in open spaces with insufficient LiDAR returns; search and rescue, disaster response/relief, caves, tunnels and 3D terrain mapping are suggested future uses, not tests they ran. Not stored or shown.
title: A one-motor drone that sees in every direction as it flies
description: A drone with one motor and two blades steers by speeding up and slowing the motor in each turn, which tilts the blades. The body itself spins as it flies. A laser distance sensor stands upright on the body, and that spin lets the laser sweep the ceiling, the floor and all around, so no spot is left unseen.
capability: A small drone with only one motor can now see in every direction at once and fly itself through a forest or an underground car park, with no satellite signal and no computer on the ground, and it keeps flying when something hits it. Tests reached more than six metres a second. This is a research prototype, not a product yet.
useCases: Mapping a place where satellite navigation does not work, such as an underground car park or the space under the trees in a forest, and planning a path from that map even while hovering.
Flying itself through a cluttered indoor space with pillars, doorways and overhead pipes, even when it bumps into something along the way.
The team's goal: helping with search and rescue, disaster response, and mapping of caves or tunnels. Named as a hoped-for use; not a test they ran.
body:
Usual drones need several motors to steer, and they often add extra cameras or spinning mounts so they can see more. This design uses the spin of the body itself, so one motor and one laser distance sensor can both fly the aircraft and look in every direction. All of the mapping, steering around obstacles and flight control ran on the aircraft, with no satellite navigation, no outside tracking cameras and no computer on the ground.

In tests it flew itself at more than six metres a second through dense woods and through an underground car park with pillars, doorways and overhead pipes. It also flew fast figure-eights and flipped in the air, staying much closer to its planned path than the usual control method in the study. A light carbon-fiber frame, plus a controller that notices bumps, kept it flying steadily when a ball was dropped on it while it hovered, and when it flew into obstacles and pushed them aside. It weighs about 1.12 kilograms and hovered for a measured fifteen minutes and fifty seconds.

This is a research prototype. There is no product, maker or price. The team says it still needs to find its place more reliably in open spaces where a laser has few surfaces to bounce off. They name search and rescue, disaster response, caves, tunnels and three-dimensional mapping of terrain as hoped-for uses, not tests they have run.
